_about: Care info for each KIND of plant, shared by every plant of that kind in plants.json. Edit text here and it changes for every matching plant. Months use Jan..Dec. 'seasonal' says what the plant looks like each month (drives the 3D view). 'care' entries show on the plant card and become tasks in This week during the months listed. Optional task fields (repeat, tip, after, afterDays, before) are explained in data/README.md.

dogToxic.detail: ASPCA: toxic to dogs (paeonol). Vomiting, diarrhea, depression.

species.wildlife: Single and semi-double flowers feed bees. Ants on the buds are harmless and don't need treatment.

cutFlower.when: Cut at the soft-bud ("marshmallow") stage: the bud shows color and feels soft in the center when you squeeze it gently.
cutFlower.how: Cut in the cool morning and leave at least 3 leaves on each stem so the plant can recover. Put the stems straight into water. Buds can be dry-wrapped and kept in the fridge for a week or more and opened later.
cutFlower.confidenceWhy: The harvest stage comes from Iowa State Extension. The fridge-storage tip is common florist practice that I didn't confirm on that page.

care.text: Put up a grow-through ring or hoop before the red shoots reach about 6 inches. It's much harder to add supports later.
Give about 1 inch of water a week when it's dry. Water at the base, not on the leaves, which helps keep leaf blotch and mildew down.
Spread a thin layer of compost around the plant, not on top of the crown. Skip high-nitrogen fertilizer, which gives floppy stems and fewer flowers.
Cut-flower window: soft-bud stage (see Cut flowers).
Deadhead spent flowers down to a leaf. Leave the foliage standing: it feeds the roots for next year's blooms.
Check for leaf blotch (purple-brown spots and blotches) and powdery mildew (white coating). Neither usually kills the plant. The fix is the fall cleanup below.
September is the time to divide or move peonies. Replant so the pink buds ("eyes") sit no more than about 2 inches below the soil. Planting too deep is the #1 reason peonies stop flowering.
After frost, cut every stem to the ground. Remove and bag the leaves and the mulch right under the plant. Don't compost them, because the leaf blotch fungus overwinters on that debris.

species.confidenceWhy: The fall cleanup and disease steps come from Ohio State, Illinois and UConn. Planting depth and division timing come from Missouri Botanical Garden and are standard, well-agreed advice.

dogToxic.detail: ASPCA: mildly toxic to dogs. Mild stomach upset and skin irritation.

species.wildlife: Single and open-centered dahlias feed bees and butterflies late into fall. Fully double forms offer little pollen.

cutFlower.when: Cut when the flower is about 3/4 to fully open. Dahlia buds do NOT keep opening after they're cut.
cutFlower.how: Cut long stems in the cool early morning or evening, just above a pair of side buds, so the plant keeps branching. Put stems straight into water. Many growers dip the cut ends in hot water (about 160–180°F) for about a minute to help vase life. Expect about 3–5 days in the vase. More cutting means more flowers.
cutFlower.confidenceWhy: Growers widely agree on cutting at the open stage. I couldn't find a university page that states it, so the details come from commercial growers.

care.text: Optional: pot up tubers indoors in mid-April, about 4 weeks before the safe planting date (mid-May), for earlier flowers.

Plant tubers after the last frost, once the soil feels warm (late May–early June), 4–6 inches deep with the eye facing up. Set stakes now so you don't spear tubers later. Don't water until sprouts appear, which prevents rot.
Pinch out the center tip when plants are about 12 inches tall with 3–4 sets of leaves. You get bushier plants and more, longer cutting stems.
Water deeply 1–2 times a week in dry spells. Mulch keeps roots cool.
Use a low-nitrogen, higher-potassium feed (for example a tomato-type organic fertilizer) every few weeks. Too much nitrogen gives weak stems.

Watch for thrips (streaky, distorted petals), earwigs and slugs (ragged holes), spider mites in heat, and powdery mildew in late summer. Organic first: hand-pick, trap earwigs in rolled newspaper, and hose mites off the undersides of leaves.
Cut-flower window: cut often (see Cut flowers). Deadhead anything you don't cut.

Dig tubers 1–2 weeks after frost blackens the leaves. Cut stems to about 4–6 inches, label each clump (variety or color), let them dry a few days, and store below 50°F but above freezing in slightly damp vermiculite, wood shavings or sand.
Check stored tubers every month or so. Toss soft or rotting ones. Lightly mist any that are badly shriveled.

species.confidenceWhy: Digging and storage come from UNH Extension and hardiness from Missouri Botanical Garden. Pinching and feeding are standard grower practice rather than from those pages.
species.notes: Not winter-hardy in Zone 7a. Tubers must come out of the ground each fall.

Leave the rosettes green over winter. Don't bury the crowns under heavy mulch, or they'll rot.

Yellow leaves with green veins (interveinal chlorosis) has two common causes. If it starts on the OLDER, lower leaves (and often turns red), it's usually magnesium deficiency. If it starts on the NEWEST leaves at the shoot tips, it's usually iron that the plant can't take up because the soil pH is too high. Test the soil at the plant before adding anything.

species.notes: Soil: your blueberries sit on the edge of soil Zones A and B. Zone B tested pH 4.9, which is in the blueberry range, but it was also low in calcium and magnesium, high in aluminum and slightly high in lead. Low pH makes aluminum and lead more available to plants, and UMass says pH 6.5–7 minimizes lead uptake. Don't grow other food crops in Zone B until the metals follow-up test is done.

care.text: Snap or cut spears at 6–8 inches tall. Don't harvest in year 1, harvest about 2 weeks in year 2, then 6–8 weeks from year 3 on. Stop when spears get pencil-thin.
Let the ferny fronds grow all summer, because they feed next year's crowns. Weed carefully, since the roots are shallow.
Cut the dead brown ferns to the ground in late fall or early spring. Removing them in fall reduces asparagus beetle eggs.
Top-dress with compost each spring.
